headline: A 34-Inch Bass Off the Pool, and Blues Chewing Through Higgins Beach
subhead: The incoming tide at Biddeford Pool is still the best hour in this state, and the bluefish have finally shown up in numbers worth chasing.
body_markdown:
Half past five Tuesday morning, I'm standing on the rocks at the mouth of Biddeford Pool watching a guy from Saco fight a bass that had no business eating a pencil popper in six feet of water. Thirty-four inches, fat as a football, came off a white Gibbs Pencil Popper worked with short jerks right through the seam where the incoming current bends around the ledge. That fish had been sitting in the deeper hole waiting for the tide to push bait through the gut, and when it turned, he ate. That's the Pool in a nutshell — you wait for the water to start climbing, you work that current seam where it funnels past the rocks into the inner basin, and if there's bait around, something eats. Best hour of the day on this whole stretch of coast, and it hasn't changed in thirty years.

The good news this week is the bluefish finally showed some teeth. Higgins Beach has had blues working the outer bar on the last two hours of the incoming, chopping through pogies and sand eels hard enough that you can see the slicks from the parking lot. I had one morning where the water just turned nervous — bait skipping, gulls dropping — and I put a Deadly Dick tin through the middle of it and came tight before it hit bottom. Three fish, biggest maybe six pounds, in about fifteen minutes, then it shut off like someone flipped a switch. That's blues for you. They don't linger and they don't apologize. If you're throwing metal at Higgins, go with something that casts far and sinks fast — a 2-ounce Hopkins or a Kastmaster in silver — because these fish are chasing bait on top and you need to get in the water column before they move off the bar.

Striper fishing overall has been honest work, not a gift. The water up here is still running cool enough that the bass haven't gone full nocturnal like they have from the Cape south — that's the one advantage of fishing above Portland right now, the fish are still willing to feed in daylight instead of only after dark. But you're not walking up and slaying them on every tide. Prouts Neck has been the most consistent spot when the wind sits out of the southwest, which it did most of last week — that wind pushes bait tight against the rocks on the ocean side and the bass follow it in. I've done well there on a black Danny plug worked slow along the edge of the structure, right at the last two hours of the ebb when the water's draining off the rockweed and everything gets funneled into the pockets. Cape Elizabeth's ledges have given up a few fish too, mostly at first light on Sluggos rigged weightless, drifted through the washes.

Mackerel are still schooled up off the Wells Harbor breakwater and around the Ogunquit rocks, and that's worth your time even if it's not glamorous — a string of Sabiki jigs or a small diamond jig dropped through a school will fill a cooler in twenty minutes, and fresh mackerel strip is about the best bass bait you can hang on a hook if you want to fish bait instead of iron. Flounder are showing in the usual soft-bottom spots at the mouths of the Kennebunk and the Saco, especially on the last of the incoming when the water's warmed a touch and they slide up onto the flats — bloodworms or clam on a simple two-hook flounder rig, fished slow and patient.

Cod are still there if you want to make the run — the deeper ledges off Cape Elizabeth in 60 to 90 feet have kept producing on diamond jigs and bait, though it's a smaller-boat game this time of year with the pleasure traffic thick on weekends.

We're building toward the new moon, and that means the tides are getting some shoulders to them — stronger push, stronger drain. That's usually good news for the Pool and for any current-fed spot on this stretch, because more water moving means more bait getting displaced and more reason for bass to sit on the seams and wait. If the southwest wind holds into the weekend, I'd be at Prouts Neck on the dropping tide and at Biddeford Pool right as the water starts to climb — that first hour of push has been the most dependable window all summer. Higgins is worth a scouting run too, but don't build a whole trip around the blues; they're moving targets right now, here one tide and gone the next. Bring the metal, bring the plugs, and don't be surprised if you have to cover some rock to find where they're stacked up today.
